projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Fickel was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran John A. Fickel, also known as Jack. Mr. Fickel served with the U.S. Army. He served in the Pacific theater, and he is a veteran of Pearl Harbor. Jack's highest rank was Sergeant. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Fickel's home in Parma Heights, Ohio, on February 6th, 2002. Jack was 79 at the time of this recording. So when did you join the Army?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I was in the chemical warfare. Most people never even heard of our type of an organization, in chemical warfare. We were a -- a mortar company. We had 4.2 chemical mortars. That's almost similar in size to 105 millimeter, and they -- it was the only mortar that the armed forces had that had a -- a lands and grooves in the barrel, so when you dropped a shell down the barrel it had a -- an expansion ring on the back of the shell. The shells were 32-pounders. It would -- it would go into the lands and grooves and come out spinning, so you could hit a target. Regular mortars, they come out lobbing and you don't know where they're going to land, see. But in our type of gun we could shoot -- go about a mile, and it hit our target. And it was very important that it be that way, because we were basically chemical warfare, gas, like mustard gas and different poison gasses that we use -- would use in case we had to use it in retaliation against an enemy who would be using it against us.

So we always carried gas wherever we went in the battle, because we had to have it just for our own protection, but we never used it. Absolutely never used it. But we also had high explosive shells. It wasn't long after Pearl Harbor, I guess it was about a year later, maybe more, they were getting ready to go into Saipan, and -- for an invasion of Saipan, and they had just loaded six LST's. They had them lined up along the dock one after another in a -- in a big row, you know, extending out from the dock six right in a row. And we had just finished loading them up, and it was on a Sunday, and they had some Hawaiian people, civilians, they were welding on the deck for some reason, and they burned threw the deck, and our outfit had just left for the day and while these guys were welding on the deck and burnt through the deck and blew up all six LST's. At that time they almost called it like a second Pearl Harbor, the way the explosion was enormous, you know. Thousands and thousands of rounds of ammunition went up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your home town before you joined the army?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Right here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right here in --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Right in the west side of Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And when did you join, when did you -- were you drafted or did you sign up?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I joined. I turned 18 in February of 1941. In fact, I just had my birthday this past week, and I joined the Army on July 25th. I was 18. My mother had to sign for me. And after she signed for me I went down and -- to the federal building and I got sworn in, and they marched us immediately, practically, across the street to the terminal tower and got on a train and went up to Fort Hayes, Columbus. I was in Fort Hayes, Columbus, only a few days and they had me on a train. Now, incidentally, I had my own civilian clothes. I never issued a uniform. You know, all I did was sit there and eat their meals, waiting to see what was gonna happen.

Anyway, in a few days they put us on a train for Fort McDowell, California, which is a little island in the San Francisco Bay right past Alcatraz, and I was there -- that's where I got my first medical -- physical examination. And I was only there a couple days and they had me on a -- the President Taft liner, which had just been converted to a troop ship, and went to Hawaii. So from the day I sworn in on July 25th I was in Hawaii on August 11th, that's 17 days. Now, of them 17 days eight of them was travel time, four days in a train across the country and four days on a ship to get to Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you got your training in Hawaii, then, your basic training?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: My own outfit gave me my basic training in six weeks. It was a hectic six weeks, I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What -- what outfit were you in?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Chemical warfare. That -- first time -- at that time it was called --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you attached to anybody?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: We were part of the Hawaiian department.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was life like in Hawaii --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Well, it was great -- great until the war started. It was great. You know, I was lucky too. When I joined the Army the recruiter here said, he says, "You know, " he says, "you're fortunate," he says, "You have some choices here." He says, "Where do you want to go?" He says, "You have four places you can pick from," he said, "either Panama, Philippine Islands, the Hawaiian Islands, or you stay here in the United States," you know. So I said, "Hawaii." Fortunately for me it worked out. And so that's where I went. Then he said, "Oh, you --" also he says, "you have your choice of branch of service," you know, and he gave me the whole litany of what branches were available, you know, from the infantry on down or up, whatever you want. Anyway, I picked chemical warfare, and I got what I asked for, which is very unusual for the Army. They tell you one thing and do something else.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what kind of things did you do there in Hawaii when you first got there for -- for entertainment?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Well, we used to -- after we finished our basic training, our boot camp, we were given class "A" passes. We could go to town every night, you know. We'd get on a taxi and go into town -- if you can afford it, or hitchhike, whatever, you know. You could go into town every night if you want as long, as you're there for reveille the following morning, you got to stand up for role call, you know. And -- but we'd never usually go, because we never had that kind of money. Heck, I went on $21 a month, and they give me 21 percent overseas increase, you know, for overseas pay.

So anyway, I -- we would go to town mostly on weekends, you know, you stand inspection on every Saturday morning and then you take off, and you didn't have to be back until Monday, actually, for reveille. So we -- that's how we always spent our time, you know, other than learning the Army way of life. You know, you had all the -- the drilling and marching, and you had to learn the chemical warfare business too. You had to learn all the gasses, how to use them, when to use them. And we used to train other people for how to handle gas with gas masks, you know. That was our business.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were at Fort Shafter; is that right?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: No, I was in Schofield Barracks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were in Schofield Barracks, because Clarence was at Fort Shafter, I believe.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Clarence, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So was there a feeling of -- and incidentally, when I ask these questions you can go on as long as you want. There's -- don't worry, I've got plenty of tape. Was there a feeling of tension because of what was happening around the world and what was happening between America and Japan?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Not really. Not really. It was just, I would say, maybe a month before -- actually before the bombing of Pearl that we were all put on alert, the whole island was put on an alert. An alert means that you could still go to town and do your thing every day, but you could never leave everybody go at once. You had to always have a squad left at the barracks in case of an emergency. That's all the alert meant. But I felt -- I never felt any tension, no, not really at all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So there weren't any rumors or thoughts that possibly Pearl Harbor --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- could be hit because --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There wasn't --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: So if every -- I mean, if the big brass, like in Washington, knew about it, they kept it a pretty good secret, but I think most Pearl Harbor guys do believe that they did know this was going to happen. It was the only way they could unite the United States to go to war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Do you think that's --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Because the United States, up until that time, was actually a pacifist nation.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you think it was by design, then, that the carriers were off on assignments when the -- when the attack came?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I don't think there was any design. I think it was just a matter of luck, really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So basically we knew -- you think that --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I think they knew but maybe didn't know exactly when.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When -- and -- do you think they knew that Pearl Harbor would be hit, though?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I understand, from what I read, that Churchill knew ahead of time, but he didn't want to open his mouth either, because he needed the United States in the war to fight their war for them -- or fight their war with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think I've heard that too. December 6th, do you remember what you were doing?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: It was a Saturday. Yeah. Not much of anything. After we did our inspection we were on our own on Saturday morning. We -- we didn't do much of anything on Saturday and Sunday. It was our days -- like our day off. So I -- we really did nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you go to Honolulu that night?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Not -- no. No. Because I was eating breakfast that Sunday morning when the -- when the plane came over our area. I got a map downstairs of -- of -- of Oahu. I don't know if you remember what it looks like, picture it in your mind. See, here's the island. See -- see, this area down here, the southern part of the island, would be Pearl Harbor, and over here in this corner would be Kaneohe Naval Air Station, see, and right up here would be the Kolekole Pass, you know, the opening in the mountains. The first wave of the Japanese planes that came in came over this way, and they came through the pass, and another one kept on going and came around up into the harbor this way, you know. But the ones that came -- nothing came in on the first wave this way direct, because the Japanese Navy was up in this area, and they didn't come down directly on the north shore, which would be the windward side of the island. They went around and they come in through the Kolekole Pass, flew overland. Some came down -- up around -- up into the harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where would Schofield Barracks be, right about --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Right about here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's what I thought, because I think we drove over and looked at it.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Yeah. Right about here. Actually 28 miles, I think, at that time, from Honolulu. And Pearl Harbor is just west of Honolulu. Anyway, they come through Kolekole Pass. We were eating breakfast in our barracks when they came over, and right across the street from our barracks is a PX, and right behind the PX is an enormous water tank, you know, and I -- it was water that they -- you know, they fill up for the city of Honolulu and Kauai and all them other little towns, you know, and it was a enormous tank, and they dropped a bomb on it, and we say it was the first bomb that hit the island, you know, and missed the tank. And we couldn't imagine how they missed that tank. But that's where the first volley of planes came in from that area, right over the pass.

So I was just there just, you know, for December 7th this time. We were up at the -- well, it's funny, you know, and I -- of course I had my family with me, and just my son-in-law and myself went to -- to the -- go up and -- and this friend of mine who was in my outfit that I had met over there, you know, we had planned on meeting a few of our guys from my outfit. We met over there. Anyway, him and his wife and my son-in-law and myself, we went up to Kolekole. I went up to Schofield Barracks, and we -- when we got to the gate you put the mirrors under their -- under the car, you know, opened the trunk and opened the hood, then told us we couldn't go in. And I -- we said, "We're Pearl Harbor survivors, you know, what the heck, we were stationed here," you know, "why can't we go in?" And he says, "Well, unless you have somebody to vouch for you, you can't go in" because of the -- the fear everybody had, you know. I says, "Well that's a bunch of baloney."

I used different words than that. And anyway, the -- it was the next morning that -- when I -- this was, like, I think December the 2nd when we went up there. And it was on December 3rd when we -- when I registered for the convention, and I got hold of Chappell (ph), our national President, and I told him, I says, "Hey," I says, "we went up to Schofield and they wouldn't let us in." I said, "What's the story," you know. He says, "They wouldn't let you in," and I says, "No." He says, "How many were you?" I says, "Well, there was two survivors and two family," you know. He says, "you go back tomorrow," you know. He says, "If you can't get in tomorrow, you make sure you let me know." So we went back the next day. We went up to the gate, and they did the same thing, you know, and they says, "Go on in," and like, "Oh," I said, "great." You know, I was looking for an argument, and I says, "Do we need an escort?" He says, "No. You got the freedom of the post."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: So I talked to the right guy, anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I guess so.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: And we had the freedom of the post, so we went up to Kolekole Pass and looked around, you know, and it's a lot different now. Everything's different up there, you know. I went to my barracks, and my barracks is still there, yet everything's changed. Hell, they -- they got all kinds of on-post housing now. We didn't have any when I was there. I don't know where the guys with their -- went with their wives, in town or whatever, but they had no on-post housing at all for families, you know. And we slept in dormitories. We had two floors, two platoons, and like 120 guys, and we slept in a dormitory, and when we went up to see our barracks, same building, everything's beautiful about it, you know, a lot more trees have grown around there, and I stood there, and I was talking to a couple of GI's that were there, it's not chemical warfare anymore there, you know, in that building anyway, and talked to a couple of the guys that were there, and I said, "This is amazing," and he said, "What?" I says, "Look up at that window," I said, "there's a lamp in the window," you know.

He says, "Oh, yeah." And I says, "Oh, and curtains on the window?" He said, "Sure." I said, "It wasn't like that when I was there." I said, "It is just a plain dormitory, you know, just rows of beds." He goes, "It's all rooms now," and I said, "Good Lord. This is the Army?" You know, it wasn't my Army, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So December 7th you were eating breakfast?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: We were eating breakfast. Yeah. It was just before -- well, we eat -- I guess we went in there maybe 7:30 to eat, you know, because you eat -- they give us a couple of hours to get up and eat, and because we were on our own on weekends. Yeah, and then -- then the planes came over. We watched them, saw their nice big red ball on the side. Yeah, they were flying like -- you know, like that, and you could see the pilots's faces as they went by, because they were pretty low.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you know right away it was Japanese planes, or did you think it was --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Not right away, no. It -- when -- when we saw the red ball, then we knew. But we were wondering what the hell -- what the hell they doing here, and then all of a sudden, boom, the bomb hit across the street, and then we knew what was going on, we were being, we thought, invaded. That was my job for the next week -- well, when that -- when it first happened, you know, the first thing they did was give us our -- our guns and ammunition. Our guns at the time, I was carrying a sidearm, a .45 Colt automatic, you know, and they give me my gun and three clips, which is 21 rounds, seven rounds to a clip. That's all we had.

And they said, "Got out and get lost for -- until we find out what's going on," you know, because that's what we did, we assembled later in the day. And then -- then we were put to work. You know, they come in the second time, the second wave -- like I say, the first wave came around the side and behind, the first one -- the second one came straight in, you know. And that was about -- oh, around an hour later, closer to 9:00. I don't know what time it was. Maybe you know more than I do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've heard a lot about it. When you went out there with your -- your guns did they want you to be shooting at the planes, they want you to look for invaders?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: We were -- well, we didn't know what to do, actually. We didn't -- really didn't know what to do. We just were told to get scarce, you know, just don't bunch up together, in case there's an invasion, and then we would get together later on in the day, and that's what happened. Then all -- all we did was group together and wait for -- to be told what to do next. We didn't know what the heck to do, actually. We never prepared for something like this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you take any shots at any of the planes coming over?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Hmm-mm. Well, all we had was a .45 automatic gun, you know, it's good for maybe 50 feet, if you're lucky. It's hard to hit a target with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've heard stories of in the excitement that some guys even shot with their .45's --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- thinking they could do something.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: No, I don't know of any of our guys did that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So could you see much of what was happening off in the distance?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: No, we were too far away from Pearl. I couldn't see none of Pearl Harbor. I saw smoke rising and all that kind of stuff, you know, but other than that, there was just a couple days later before we got down there, because they were using us as riot patrols, our chemical warfare, you know, because we had the tear gas and everything else in case of anything going to happen of that nature, and nothing happened. A lot of Japanese on that island. Then, you know. There's more now, but there was a lot of them then, and you didn't know who was enemy and who wasn't. So they used us for -- they -- they called it riot patrol, but there was just actually to stop any disturbances that might occur, which never happened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along okay with the Japanese before the attack?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Fine. Fine. One of my good friends, he lives in California now, I met him over there too. Well, he was in the -- he was in the engineers, which was -- they had barracks right across the street from my outfit, down a little bit, a little further on, where there's an 18-hole golf course at Schofield. I -- if you were there you saw it. And they're not there anymore either, them barracks. He was going with a Japanese girl over there couldn't speak English. And I says, "How did you manage that," you know, I couldn't never figure that one out either.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And what was the feelings like, after the attack, of the Japanese people that lived there?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: We didn't think about it. I didn't, anyway. I don't know of any other guys -- I mean there was no enmity that I could think of against the people there, but you just -- you just were careful, because you didn't know who you were looking at or talking to. Heck, after -- even after that, when I would go into town, I would go up on the -- the Pali Road, you know, Lukalana (ph) Road, the pali Pass is what they call, you know, and a little way up the street just outside of Honolulu is a -- a Japanese house that had room service, and we would -- I would -- every time I went on pass for an overnighter I would stay at her house. It cost me three bucks a night. And I -- in her house I saw she had like a Shinto shrine for herself, like an altar that -- you know, for themselves, and nice people. They didn't create any problems that I knew of.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, you say eventually -- When did you get down to see what had happened in the harbor?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: It took about four or five days, something like that, after. Then we went down. Well, I went down, because I was driving a truck at the time, and we were going all over the -- we would go into the ordnance depot, load up the truck with ammunition, and we were performing ammunition dumps all over the island, because we were looking for an invasion and more bombing, and if they hit the ordnance depot they would have wiped out all our arms, you know, all our ammunition, so the first thing we did was create ammunition dumps all over. So I did get into town then, you know, but it took about four days or five days that -- before I got down, actually, to see the -- the scene at Pearl Harbor itself. And Pearl Harbor along the road at that time was right along the road. I mean, there's Pearl Harbor and Hickman Field was right next to each other, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what did you see when you went down there?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: There was still smoke and burning, fire, wreckage, you know. You didn't know what you were looking at, just -- just everything was up -- in upheaval, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any particular feeling when you saw what you saw there?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Crying, because we knew how many -- didn't know how many, but we knew there was a awful lot of dead people.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So how long did you remain on Hawaii?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I was there -- I stayed on the island, then, until February 1st -- no, it was in January when we left, but on February 1st I made my first beach landing in Kwajalein in the Marshall Islands.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Can you describe that.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: That was on my birthday. You know, Kwajalein is an island only a mile and a half long. It's about 800 yards wide, 11 foot high. Highest point on the island is 11 foot above sea level, I think almost including the trees. But a lot of palm trees, you know. But we took the island in three days. And when they got done they counted over 4,000 dead Japanese, and we lost just a couple hundred guys. It was -- I don't know if it was just a rest and rehabilitation area for them guys or not, but they were pretty well dug in. They had all kind of pillboxes and caves, you know -- not caves, but tunnels. No caves.

There's no altitude for caves, you know. Yeah, that was our first one. Then we went -- we were in Palau, and our outfit went to the Philippine Islands and Okinawa. Actually, I think there were -- I was in three of 'em, but I think there were five battles that the -- my outfit was in. They got three presidential citations, and we only had 120 men and three officers, a captain and two lieutenants. And over that period of time -- I wasn't with them all the time, you know, but over that period of time had over 500 man turnover in that one little two platoon outfit. As they were getting killed they were replacing them. 500 -- I under -- I understood 542, I was told. So they went through quite a bit of hell, really. But I ended up on Guam, and I was in Guam for nine months then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it a regular mortar unit, then, for most of the action?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: For all of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. But you continued to carry the chemical weapons with you?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Always. Well that was part of our mortar unit, the -- the weapons. The chemical -- the chemical weapons and the -- we never used them, though, but high explosives, the deadly -- it was a deadly mortar. I think the Marines got them now, because we fought with the Marines too, and they loved it. Good gun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any vivid memories of any of those actions that you talked about?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: It's stuff that you don't like to talk about, you know. Who wants to talk about a lot of dead people.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think the -- well, that's the kind of thing the Library of Congress is interested in. If you want to share any of that you're welcome to. I mean, that's totally up to you.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Well, what does that say, you know, I mean, they come at you, you shoot back at 'em, people die on both sides. The first man that I saw killed, we were in a group like I'm talking here, there was about six of us, you know, but it was not a close together group, it was wide around, you know, and this artillery shell came in, and the one guy, his name was Hoffman, when it landed he disappeared. And he -- none of us even got nothing. It seemed that the shell hit at an angle, like, you know, they'd come down and all the momentum went away. But it hit him and blew him to pieces. Never found any of him. That was the first guy I saw killed. And he was maybe six foot away from me, with an artillery shell. Stuff like that you don't want to remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I -- I know, I understand it's painful for you, but I think that's the important things that people need to understand about war.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I think -- I think most people do. A lot of people die, you know. Just like -- just like they're in -- right now in Afghanistan. People die. Desert Storm. Desert Storm was a snap. They say they went to war, there was 100 hours, you know, mine was four years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call, getting letters from home, anything like that, any specific memories?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Oh, we always had mail call. Mail was always coming in. They were very good about the mail.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. And you couldn't write a whole lot back home, right?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: You write what you want, but it never got through, because it was it was all censored. I mailed my album home, it was even censored.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: An album of your --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: My picture album, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of things did they censor out of that?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Well, there was one picture in particular that they took -- I think it was stolen because somebody else wanted it. I don't think it was censored because of its military value, you know. But I can remember -- I can't -- really can't remember what the heck it is. I got a space in my album where it was, and I got -- I wrote in white ink "A bunch of --" you know, "You dirty crooks" or something like that. But I think somebody stole it because they wanted it for themselves.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of -- go ahead.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Most of my pictures are in there, like family and my guys in the outfit, you know, personal pictures of that nature. Nothing military. There's some pictures in there of some of the, like, Japanese flags they got, some guys are wearing Japanese hats and that kind of stuff, you know, just to pose.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would the people back home write to you? Did they send you any packages or anything?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: My mother was always sending me packages. That's the only person I ever got mail from, was my mother. Nobody else, for me personally. Of course, my father had been dead for -- already for years. My dad, he died in 1931. He was only 44 years old. And my brother was already in the Army. He was drafted. And there was my sister and my mother. That was all. My sister got married too, and her husband, my brother-in-law, he was drafted. He went to Europe. My brother had it really made, though. They drafted him and put him in an MP escort guard company. He was escorting prisoners of war, like Italian prisoners of war from the East Coast and the -- the potato country and the corn country, you know, the guys worked there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That sounds like decent duty, especially with the Italians?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: But near the end, though, he got -- they shipped him to New Guinea, so he -- he ended up over there too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember if you had a chance to do anything for entertainment, anything to relieve the tension over there?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Oh, yeah. In fact, our company commander got in big trouble over it. We had what they call a company fund, you know, out of every one of our pays we contributed to a company fund, and it was all money of ours, you know, that they all kept getting over -- kept for the two years there it was all gathering dust, you know, growing, because everybody contributed, nobody didn't, and we had a luau on our grounds, our company grounds. We put a -- about a six foot tall canvas wrap around the perimeter of our outfit, you know, on the grounds, and we had a -- a luau. In fact, I had to help -- I helped dig the -- the hole, you know. I don't know how -- if you know how luau is made. Do you know?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I went to one when I was over there. I assume it's the same.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I had to dig -- I was part digging the hole, you know, they dig the hole and they put the hot -- white hot -- as hot as they can get it lava rock in the hole, and then they cover the rock with ti leaves. You know, the -- the ti leaves are -- it's a big leaf. And they -- they cover their hot rocks with ti leaves, they put the pig in it, you know, then they cover the pig with ti leaves. That's t-i for ti. And they cover the pig with ti leaves, and then they cover that all with the hot lava rock and then load it with dirt, fill it up. And it takes six -- between six and eight hours, and they take the pig out, and it's all done, roasted. Fine, fine food. Then we would hollow out a pineapple -- you know, pineapple, when you pick 'em in Hawaii, are twice as big as the kinds -- the ones you find here, and you don't get 'em there -- you don't pick 'em there until they're ripe, you know, and they don't taste the same. I don't know if you had any fresh pineapple over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think we did.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: And if you did you had to notice the difference. You had to notice the difference. Anyway, we would hollow out the core -- snap off the top, hollow out the core, you know, and they'd fill it with booze. So that was our luau. And we had -- what -- his name was Howie something. I can't -- I don't know if it was Howie Long or something like that, a -- a troupe of dancing girls and their -- and their musicians that we hired to come, and they entertained us in our mess hall. We had a wonderful time. Everybody got plastered. And the post commander said, "Never again will this happen," not only to our outfit, but to any outfit on the post, because that created a hell of a lot of animosity, "Well, if they can do it, why can't we," you know, that kind of a thing. So it quit it for everybody. We were the first one to do it and got away with it. But that was one of the deals that we did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was in Hawaii? Was that when you were in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: In Hawaii, in my outfit. We had a great time. We spent a lot of money on it, but what the heck, that's what it was for. We were saving it up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally get home?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I got my discharge October 25th of '45. It's four years and three months from when I joined. And I was discharged out of Guam. I was on Guam for nine months, and then from Guam -- Guam we went to Saipan to get the ship to come home. It took 28 days on a Kaiser ship. And it went -- come up onto Fort Lewis, Washington, right out of Seattle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about your reunion with your family?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: There was only my mother and -- my dad died, like I said, in 1931, and she remarried in 1944 to a man that she new practically all her life, his wife had passed away, you know, and I knew the guy, I didn't know him real well, and when I came home I didn't even know where to go. I had to get the cabbie -- it was late at night when I come home, and I gave the cabbie the address, you know, and I didn't know where it was. But he found the house, and I went up there, and I -- it was, like I say, like 11' clock at night by the time I got there, wrapped on the door, and they come to the door and they saw who I was and they almost broke my neck getting me in the house, grabbed ahold of me and pulled me in, you know, and there was only two of them, my mom and my stepfather. So it was -- just for the three of us it was quite a reunion, really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about Pearl Harbor do any other strong, vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: About the harbor itself? No. It was -- We were under military law. It was martial law immediately after the -- the bombing attack. If you went to town, like we always did, if you went into a bar, if you got -- when you got your drink, it came to you mixed. You couldn't get a unmixed drunk, you know, you -- and you got our full ounce of booze, and you were limited to, like, three of them, because they were lined up outside waiting to come in, the guys, you know. And you were limited to, like, three of them. And periodically the -- the government would send guys in just like me to sit down, order a drink, and they would pour it into a flask of their own and they'd take it out and examine it to make sure that we got our full ounce of whiskey, because they were cheating, you know, watering down the booze.

And prostitution at the time was legal in the islands, so there -- about everybody -- after anybody went into one of the hotels for prostitution they would -- when they came out they had to go in and get a prophylactic immediately. There was an MP making sure that you would get your prophylactic. They wanted no disease. But like I say, it was strictly legal -- strictly legal, and the prices were -- were by law -- they made a law, you know, what they could charge. It was $4 a person. But they had to have it. There was too many men, you know, really not enough women.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now how long was Hawaii a tense place to be after December 7th?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Not long.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The tension sort of eased after so long?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: It -- it eased off. Once they found out that there was no invasion coming right away, like we really expected it, you know, then it eased off real quick, I would say. Of course a lot of more guys got there too, you know. I mean, they filled the island up with people. There was a lot of work going on. You know they had to get all them ships up out of the harbor and get them, what they could, out of there and repair what they could, you know, a lot of heavy work going on. They brought in a lot of construction people from the mainland who were not in the service, private contractors, you know, to do all that kind of work. But they were the only ones who had experience with that kind of stuff, to rebuild the ships.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Does anything else come to mind, any other vivid memories come to mind about the other experiences you had overseas in the other islands?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Well, it's -- it's -- war is hell, you know. War is war, what the heck, you know, when you land on the beach you do your job and then you get off and you go back and wait for the next call.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any particularly rough landings that you had?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: They were all rough. Well, you're landing and they're waiting for you. They were all rough. Look at the -- look at the job that the guys had, like, on Iwo Jima, which I was not there, and the -- the first big devastating hit we took was at Tarawa, when the Marines landed there. They lost a tremendous amount of guys, just trying to get on the beach. That's -- that's how I differentiate between the Europe and the United States and the Pacific. In Europe when they landed at Normandy it was -- Omaha Beach was -- you know, a lot of -- lot of guys got killed at Omaha Beach. Once they got up off the beach and inland there was no more beachheads, you know, no more beachheads, and they wouldn't -- just everything was on land, practically, which didn't make war any easier, you know, but all of our expeditions was -- every one was a beachhead.

Every island you come to was another beachhead. All of them. They call it island hopping. Every one was a beachhead, and beachheads are nasty, because they're waiting for you. You'd bomb 'em -- they'd bomb 'em for a few days before they land, you know. But they had so many caves and tunnels, you know, you couldn't get 'em, really. But my outfit invented the flame throwing tank. You've heard of the flame throwing tanks? Because that was our business, the flame throwers, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were they first used?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: In the Pacific on an island.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You don't remember which island?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I don't know which island, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What, someone just came up with the idea --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Because we didn't fight with tanks in my outfit, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They came up with the idea of a mounted flame thrower on a tank, because that was the only way to --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Well, my -- my barracks -- my barracks in Hawaii was divided in half, this half was chemical warfare, this half was a tank outfit. And across the street was the signal corps, where that guy Jackson was the guy that first knew that they were -- that we were getting invaded by planes, and they said that must be planes coming from the mainland, you know. They ignored his warning that those planes were coming in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the guy with the radar installation?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Then it was him? Okay.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: It was him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. And they thought it was the --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: He was billeted right across the street from us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Yeah. But he wasn't there when this was going on. He was at a radar station.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And they just dismissed it as the B-17's coming in from the mainland?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Yeah. And they were coming in unarmed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Yeah. There was a few of those -- them got shot at when they came in right?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they arrive during the height of the attack, or was it shortly after, or --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: It was almost -- the attack was immediately almost over by the time they were getting in to land. And they couldn't do nothing anyway, because they were low on fuel to begin with.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember where you were when you heard the news that FDR had died?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Yeah, I was on Guam. I was on Guam.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the feeling among the guys?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I -- I -- you know, everybody was sad, you know, but I didn't think it made that big an effect on them. Just the news came in that FDR passed, you know, but I don't think it had that much of an effect.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you think you were -- would have been part of the plans to invade Japan?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Absolutely. Absolutely. And it was a good thing they dropped the bomb, absolutely, because I don't know if -- if people -- I -- I -- they didn't -- they just didn't realize how tenacious the Japanese were. They -- they would have fought women and children against us. They were prepared for it, to use anything -- you know, they would fight to the last person almost. It was like a religion to them, die for the Emperor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you -- your reaction when you heard they had dropped the bomb, you were on Guam at that time?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Yippee. Oh, yeah, we were -- we were glad that happened. It was -- hey, you know, it's war. It's either them or us, and they weren't going to give up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Not that I can think of, unless you can think of some more questions.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I'm asking more questions than I usually ask. You don't need to wait for my questions. If you can think of anything else, I don't like to ask a lot of specific questions, because I don't know about your specific experiences, so I try to ask some general questions, hopefully trigger a personal memory, but I think I've covered most of the topics that I usually cover, so it's if you have anything else that you can remember or any memories that I haven't touched on.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: No, not really. Not really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I usually ask about buddies. Did you have any buddies?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: A lot of friends. A lot of friends. When I was on Guam I was put in charge of building up a chemical warfare depot and, like, the gas mask repair area, you know, and all that kind of stuff, and there was only myself and two other guys. And we had to build our own Quonset huts and do all the work ourselves, so obviously the three of us couldn't handle it, you know, so they assigned a -- what they call aircraft engineers to do our work for us, you know, and it was a -- a colored outfit, black -- black outfit, and in the second war they didn't use colored people at all for combat. They were there strictly as work. In the Navy they were stewards. Really, they didn't. And this -- they would give me, like, a couple of squads of guy, you -- guys every day to come over work in my depot, they built my quonset huts, you know, and between the three of us, we treated them real well, you know, and they did everything for us that we wanted. In fact, when they was done they built me a beer cooler.

They was good guys, caused no problems, you know. The fact of the matter is on the weekends, when they would -- were supposed to be off, you know, they -- their -- their -- they had white officers. Their white officers were not liked by them, you know, they lorded it over them like you wouldn't believe. And a lot of officers were like that, whether you were white or black, you know. And so I would detail a squad of guys to come over every weekend, one on Saturday and another one on Sunday. When they got there I -- they didn't have nothing to do, I said, "Just do nothing," just so they wouldn't have to work at their own outfit. So I think they appreciated that. They did a lot of stuff for us then too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any run-ins with officers, any encounters that you remember?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Never. Never.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Avoided them?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: That's the only way. You've got -- you know, you've got to be just a number, practically, you know. You just stay out of their line of site as much as you can. Do what you're told and keep your mouth shut. You know how that works.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your highest rank?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Sergeant. I came out a Corporal. I went -- I went AWOL for a couple of days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Hmm. So that's how you lost the rank?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: So I lost -- lost a stripe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why did you go AWOL?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Well, you get a three day pass and you come back in five.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just had things to do, huh?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I had things to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The rank didn't mean that much?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Nah. I didn't care, really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You just wanted out?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Right. So anyway, that was the way it worked.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Pretty much so. Do you know what these are? This is my Expert Weapons Badge. I was -- I was pretty good shooting. And this is the chemical warfare -- them are the retorts, you know, cross retorts, chemical warfare. This is the Asiatic Pacific theater, this is the Good Conduct Medal, this is the American Defense Ribbon. The star's in there because I was at Pearl Harbor. These are my three Battle Stars, and this is the Bronze Star.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Lieutenant ____ had one of those -- has. He's not here but I still have the medals.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Yeah. Do you know what the Bronze Star is?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Bronze Star. What did you get the Bronze Star for?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: You know, I didn't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it an award to the unit or --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: No, to me. When I got -- when I got -- I didn't know I had it. I really didn't never know that I was put in for the Bronze Star, and when I got my discharge in Camp Atterbury, Indiana, they held us up there for over a week trying to talk us into joining the reserves, you know, and I held out. I didn't. My buddy, who was in the Navy, he joined the Navy, he joined the reserves, and they called him back for Korea then. And I probably would have been too if I had got -- joined the reserves, you know, but I didn't join the reserves. When I got my discharge that day they handed me my Bronze Star and everything, and I go, "What the heck's this for?" He says, "It's on your discharge, you're supposed to get one," and I looked at my dis -- that's the first I saw my discharge, and I read it on there, and it said, you know, a Bronze Star per general order, blah blah blah blah. So somebody had to put you in -- put you in for it. You don't get them by yourself.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. A nice surprise.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: That's a big surprise. Yeah. I knew I had the Good Conduct Ribbon. I knew all the other ribbons I had, but I didn't know about the Bronze Star. That -- that was a shock to me. I could have got a Purple Heart, but I didn't stop to get the medical treatment.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I didn't get -- I didn't think I got hurt that bad. A grenade had blew up right on -- I practically walked on it, you know, and it got me in the groin, and it didn't damage anything, thank God, but I had the scars and everything in there, but they're probably almost gone now, too, you know, but it -- I didn't worry about it, you know, in the heat of everything going on you just didn't think. I didn't care.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you didn't even get treatment for it?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Hmm-mm. If I would have stopped and got treatment, then I would have got that, because, you know, it would have been on record then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: But I never turned myself in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well it's a shame you can't put in for it now. You told me. I believe it.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Yeah. Well I'm not worried about it. The only thing --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Library of Congress will know about it now.

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: The -- the thing that -- what was I going to say -- the thing that bothered me most about it was the five points that I didn't get toward discharge. But it ended up I didn't need 'em. My -- my -- when I got discharged I had 128 points and they were getting them out with 75 at the time, you know. But I was -- when you're stuck on an island out there it isn't that easy to get a ship home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. So you just had to stay and wait --

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Just had to wait it out. And I -- the funny part of it was about a month before my discharge I was driving a -- the truck in Guam, and I had a bunch of guys in the back, and I stopped the truck and I says let's go in and get a pop or something, you know, and because beer was rationed to you; you couldn't go into a PX and buy a beer, you know, it just didn't happen. So I stopped at the PX, it was on -- a field PX that they just set up on Guam, and stopped -- the guys got out of the truck, and I -- I was driving, and I swung sideways to the opening, you know, the door opening, and just put my feet on the fender, and on the fender there was these containers for five gallon gas supply, you know, spare gas, but the gas cans were gone. All that was there was the thing that held them in place, you know, where you strapped them on -- on the fender, and I didn't realize at that time, but my heel caught in the one, and then when I stepped down off the running board to the ground, which is about yea high, you know, this heel stayed put, you know what I mean, and it pulled it right apart, snapped it right in two.

I said all kinds of dirty things at that time. But one of the guys -- and my foot swolled up like a balloon right away. They took me down to a field hospital, which was not too far up the -- the road, you know. I sat in that hospital just about a month, almost a month. They wouldn't let me, even to go to the mess hall there in the hospital to eat, stand a bit. So after I got out of the hospital, and it was another couple of weeks of on the crutches, then they took the -- the cast off, you know, and then I could get my -- I got my discharge then. They shipped me over to Saipan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have trouble adjusting to civilian life when you got back?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Nah. The first thing I did when I got back, I went down -- it was Bennett York Buick (sp) on West 103rd and Lorraine, and I put in an order for a car, a new car, and he -- he -- they looked at me like I was out of my mind, you know, "What do you mean new car, they ain't making 'em yet," you know. And I says, "Well, they will be, and I want to be on the list for when the cars come in, I want a new car." "What kind you want?" I said, "I don't care." And I says, "And here's 100 --" I give them $100 as -- for that -- that was a lot of money then too. I give them $100 for a down payment, you know, to seal the deal, in other words. And ten months later I got a phone call, and they says, "We have a car here if you want it." I says, "I'll be right down," and I went down there, and I brought my checkbook with me, and I went down there, and they said it's a -- it was a 1946 Buick Super, and it was a real dark green in color, you know. He said, "This is one of the first cars to hit town.

You're getting it because you were the first one to put in for one," you know. And it was just ten months later, and I got this new 1946 Buick. I paid $2,360 for it, which was big bucks for a car then. They were selling not really -- 900 to $1,000 not long after that, you know. But I guess -- that's what I paid for that car, and I drove it out of the dealers, and from 103rd I went up Lorraine Street, I had to stop at the light at West 105th, and a guy wrapped on my window, you know, I says, "What do you want?" He says, "How would you like to make $800," and I says, "You've got to be kidding. I just got this thing." And I said, "No, thank you," and I went home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So he wanted to buy it from you on the spot?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: On the spot. He says, "How would you like to make $800?"

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long did you keep the car?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Let's see. I got rid of it in 1954, and it was a rust bucket when I got rid of it. Oh, it was falling -- the bumpers fell off and everything else. I had 90-some thousand miles on it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You got your money's worth out of it?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: I sure did. Well, I got my money out of it in the first month I had it, I'll tell you. Boy, was I the king of the town then, because I kept telling everybody "I got a new car coming." They said, "Mm-hmm, sure you do," you know. And then when I did show up with the new car, then, boy, they were all, "Hey, let's go for a ride," all that kind of stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Most popular guy in town?

sp.speaker: John Fickel
sp.p: Most popular guy in the west side, anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, that's great.
